# Android gets AI defenses against messaging scams, fake calls

- October 15, 2026

- 03:48 PM

- 0

Google announced new AI-powered defenses against scam messages and call-forwarding abuse on Android, currently rolling out to eligible devices.

The new measures aim to address the increased sophistication of scams targeting mobile users, including fraudulent bank alerts and voice-cloning attacks.

“Mobile scams have evolved far beyond basic robocalls and phishing texts, turning into sophisticated operations that use spoofed numbers, fake bank alerts, and AI voice cloning,” Google says .

“With scams growing harder to spot, it’s nearly impossible for users to catch every red flag themselves,” added the tech giant.

Google says its existing Phone and Messages scam detection flags more than 5 million suspected scam calls and texts monthly, but the new measures are expected to catch even more threats.

### Cloud-based scam analysis

The new protections focus on Google Messages and rely on cloud-based Gemini-backed analysis for complex conversations, scrutinizing them for signs of fraud.

The system analyzes conversations with unknown senders within the encrypted Private AI Compute environment, protecting user privacy at all times.

The new mode also adds on-device Gemini Nano (local AI model) checks for unfamiliar links using real-time web signals, plus clearer warnings before opening links from unsaved numbers.

The new cloud-based protections are currently disabled by default, allowing users to activate them.

### Other improvements

Apart from the Google Messages protection, Google has also implemented the enhancements in other areas of the Android system:

- On-device scam detection in chat notifications, previously launched on Pixel , will reach hundreds of millions more users through Android device partners later this year.

- Android’s existing sensitive-information masking is now expanding to Chrome and Android WebView, hiding login fields and payment screens during live screen sharing.

- Android blocks apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warns users before manually entered MMI forwarding codes take effect.

Google is also expanding its verified bank calls system, introduced earlier this year , adding financial institutions from more.

This system checks whether a real bank’s call center initiated an incoming call or if it is a spoofing attempt. If the verification fails, the call is automatically ended.

Google says that since June it has blocked over 3 million fraudulent calls of this kind for Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. Revolut and other global financial institutions are also supported.

Android users should upgrade to the latest release, keep apps updated, and independently verify caller/sender identities when receiving requests for account-related action or sensitive information.

## Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked

Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments.

# ARTEX AI, Claude agents used in cyberattacks on South Korean banks

- October 10, 2026

- 10:16 AM

- 0

A Chinese-speaking hacker launched cyberattacks that shook the South Korean financial sector earlier this month, using the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite and Claude agents.

The actor targeted multiple Korean banks , including Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Hana Bank, exposing clients ' personal data and credit card information, and causing system outages in some cases.

The South Korean government reacted with an emergency meeting and calls for immediate security measures for critical IT systems.

Security firm CrowdStrike confirmed the use of ARTEX AI, up until recently an open-source agentic penetration testing suite developed in China.

Researchers identified the attacker's infrastructure and found open directories with Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files, and Claude memory files.

“The ARTEX instance used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the primary LLM backend, and the threat actor supplemented this LLM with GLM-5.3 (Zhipu AI) and Grok 4.6 for additional Claude Code sessions,” CrowdStrike explained.

“The threat actor likely accessed DeepSeek via the likely LLM API proxy/reseller xcai[.]pro,” the researchers noted .

These records also provided insight into the attacker’s activities, with targets overlapping those named in previous reporting about financial-sector breaches, allowing for high-confidence linking.

Because the threat actor used the same AI tools to create a résumé, they also exposed identification, contact, and Telegram account details.

Based on information in the résumé, CrowdStrike says that the attacker may be a 26-year-old Chinese who studied at the South China University of Technology and lives in Maoming, Guangdong, China.

However, the researchers found that the attacker initially provided a date of birth in 2007. Although the personal details may belong to the individual behind the ARTEX-related activity, they are not reliable enough to confirm the threat actor’s identity.

The records show the attacker had no specific plan to monetize the data stolen from South Korean banks, and asked Claude to propose Telegram data-sales groups focused on Korea.

After confirming that ARTEX had been used in real-world attacks, the developer decided to make the project closed-source and discontinue further updates.

However, the project’s current code has been used to create English- and Korean-language derivatives , so it’s still available in its current form.
